summary: Known skin and eye irritant at concentrations above 2%. Disrupts the skin barrier and may increase transepidermal water loss with repeated use.
Rare cases of contact allergy have been reported. Not classified as a sensitiser by most regulatory bodies.
At high concentrations (>1%) may cause skin and eye irritation. EU Regulation limits cosmetic use to 1%.
source_name: EU Commission Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex V
population_context: At concentrations above 1%

summary: Animal studies suggest potential effects on the central nervous system at high oral doses; relevance to typical cosmetic exposure is unclear.
population_context: Animal data only; not demonstrated in humans

summary: Weak estrogenic activity observed in in-vitro and animal studies. Detected in breast tumour tissue, though causality is not established.
source_name: Darbre et al. 2004 Journal of Applied Toxicology
population_context: In vitro and animal data; human causality not established

summary: Estrogenic activity detected in in-vitro assays. Animal studies show effects on male reproductive system at high doses.
source_name: Routledge et al. 1998 Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology
population_context: Animal data; not demonstrated at typical cosmetic exposure levels

summary: Strongest estrogenic activity among common parabens. Classified as a suspected endocrine disruptor by the EU. Restricted in leave-on products for children under 3.
population_context: Prohibited in rinse-off products for children under 3

summary: Animal studies indicate effects on male reproductive development at doses above typical human exposure.
source_name: EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety SCCS Opinion 2011
population_context: Animal data at high doses

summary: Undisclosed fragrance mixtures may contain one or more of 26 EU-regulated fragrance allergens (e.g. linalool, limonene, cinnamal). Exact composition is typically proprietary.
population_context: Applies to any product listing 'Fragrance' or 'Parfum' without full disclosure

summary: Generic fragrance mixtures are a leading cause of contact dermatitis in cosmetic users.
population_context: Particularly in individuals with sensitive or compromised skin

summary: Detected in blood, urine, and breast milk after topical sunscreen application. In-vitro estrogenic activity observed. FDA has called for more safety data.
source_name: FDA Proposed Rule on OTC Sunscreen 2019
population_context: Systemic absorption documented; endocrine relevance at typical doses unresolved

summary: Linked to coral reef bleaching. Banned in Hawaii and several reef-protection jurisdictions.
source_name: Downs et al. 2016 Archives of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology
population_context: Aquatic/environmental impact; not a human health concern at cosmetic doses

summary: Retinol (Vitamin A) is a potent active that causes skin irritation, peeling, and photosensitivity at higher concentrations, especially in new users.
source_name: American Academy of Dermatology Clinical Guidelines
population_context: Particularly during initial use; photosensitivity risk requires SPF use

summary: A US NTP photocarcinogenicity study found tumour acceleration in hairless mice with retinyl palmitate + UV. Regulatory bodies have not classified it as a human carcinogen.
population_context: Animal data under UV exposure; relevance to human cosmetic use is uncertain

summary: IARC reclassified inhaled TiO2 nanoparticles as possibly carcinogenic (Group 2B). The inhalation route is the concern; topical/dermal application is considered safe.
population_context: Inhalation route only (e.g. spray/powder products); dermal application considered safe

summary: IARC Group 1 known human carcinogen. Direct use is prohibited in EU cosmetics; however, it may be released by formaldehyde-releasing preservatives (DMDM Hydantoin, Quaternium-15, etc.).
A formaldehyde-releasing preservative. The amount of free formaldehyde released depends on concentration and formulation. Low levels in typical cosmetics.
source_name: CIR Expert Panel Report on DMDM Hydantoin
population_context: Via formaldehyde release; not a direct carcinogen itself

summary: Animal studies show thyroid hormone disruption. FDA banned triclosan in OTC antibacterial soaps (2016). Still permitted in some cosmetics under specific limits.
source_name: FDA Final Rule: Safety and Effectiveness of Consumer Antiseptics
population_context: Animal data; banned in hand soaps; still permitted in select cosmetic categories

summary: Persistent environmental contaminant. Toxic to aquatic organisms. Found in surface water, fish tissue, and human breast milk.
source_name: Chalew & Halden 2009 Journal of the American Water Resources Association

summary: IARC Group 3 (inadequate evidence for carcinogenicity in humans). Banned in OTC cosmetics in the EU and some other markets. Controlled use in prescribed products.
population_context: Prohibited in EU cosmetics; restricted prescription use only

summary: Irritant contact dermatitis, paradoxical hyperpigmentation (ochronosis) with prolonged use, and cytotoxic effects on melanocytes reported.
Contact allergy to oxybenzone is relatively common. Reported as one of the top photoallergens in sunscreen users.
population_context: Photoallergy particularly relevant in prolonged sun exposure

summary: BHA exfoliant; causes dryness, peeling, and irritation especially at higher concentrations (>2%). EU restricts to 2% in rinse-off products and 0.5% in leave-on products.
source_name: EU Cosmetics Regulation Annex III — Salicylic Acid
population_context: Concentration-dependent; irritation more likely in sensitive skin

summary: Generally well tolerated. Rare contact allergy cases reported. At high concentrations may cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals.
source_name: CIR Expert Panel Report on Propylene Glycol

summary: IARC Group 1 human carcinogen when inhaled occupationally. Cosmetic coal tar (in anti-dandruff shampoos) is restricted; FDA permits it at 0.5-5% for OTC anti-dandruff use.
population_context: Occupational inhalation exposure; regulated cosmetic use considered lower risk

summary: EU prohibited in cosmetics as a CMR (Category 1B reproductive toxin). Animal studies demonstrate developmental and reproductive toxicity.
population_context: Prohibited in EU cosmetics

summary: Antiandrogenic effects in animal studies. Reduces testosterone and causes male reproductive tract malformations in rats.
source_name: NTP Centre for the Evaluation of Risks to Human Reproduction
population_context: Animal data

summary: Formaldehyde-releasing preservative. One of the most common causes of cosmetic-related contact allergy in the US. Releases formaldehyde continuously.
population_context: Via formaldehyde release

summary: Consistent top-ranked cosmetic allergen in patch test studies across multiple decades.
source_name: North American Contact Dermatitis Group Patch Test Results 2019-2020

summary: Probable human carcinogen (IARC Group 2B). Not intentionally added to cosmetics; forms as a by-product during ethoxylation of surfactants (e.g. SLES). FDA monitors levels.
population_context: Contaminant; not a listed ingredient; generated during manufacturing

summary: Animal studies (high oral doses) showed thyroid tumours. EU SCCS assessed topical cosmetic use (1%) as safe with some uncertainty. Not classified as carcinogen for normal use.
source_name: EU SCCS Opinion on Kojic Acid 2021
population_context: Animal data at supraphysiological doses; EU assessment supports safety at ≤1%
